articles.title: It’s Been 25 Years Since 9/11—These Are the 10 Most Powerful Stories About the Tragedy
articles.content:
Twenty-five years goes by in an instant. On Sept. 11, 2001, four planes were hijacked and pointed directly at the heart of the country, and life hasn’t been the same since. Though time can have a dulling effect, pushing those memories into a safe corner of one’s mind or lengthening the time between them, the awful visuals and lived experiences never go away.
It’s hard to believe, but a third of Americans were born after 9/11. But the effects of the attack—an enhanced surveillance state, increased airport security and military incursions around the world—are felt by everyone. Universal, too, are the stories of heroism, friendship and sacrifice that will forever mark that sad day.
With the 25th anniversary of 9/11 upon us, we put together a list of some of the most important journalism that took us through the day as it happened or examined it from the perspective of time. Ahead, we have 10 remarkable stories about Sept. 11, 2001. Some have been celebrated for decades; others you may never have read.
Read on to look back at the tragedy and perhaps find hope in some of the stories.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more news, real stories, travel, tech and trending topics all week long.
On Sept. 12, 2001, the Associated Press published a photograph of an unknown man falling headfirst from the north tower of the World Trade Center. In 2003, Esquire journalist Tom Junod set out to determine who the man was by reviewing the entire series of 12 photographs taken by AP photographer Richard Drew. The result explores collective grief and trauma and has become one of the defining pieces of journalism from the post–9/11 era.
Read more at Esquire
The title of this piece refers to the amount of time that elapsed between the first plane hitting the north tower at 8:46 a.m. and its collapse at 10:28 a.m. Eight months after the attack, the New York Times published an accounting of those 102 minutes by piecing together emails and phone calls from those trapped and killed, as well as recollections from survivors. It’s as chilling now as it was when it was first published.
Read more at The New York Times
The staff of the Wall Street Journal won the Pulitzer Prize for Breaking News Reporting in 2002 for its 9/11 coverage. That coverage included real-time reports of the planes and collapses as well as potential impacts, including to airport security and the economy, as they were happening. One particularly harrowing story is a first-person accounting of that day called “The Eye of the Storm: One Journey Through Desperation and Chaos,” by John Bussey.
You can read all of the winning coverage at the Pulitzer Prize page, below.
Read more at The Pulitzer Prizes
This narrative account, published just days after 9/11, weaves together events at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and the final moments of United Flight 93, which went down in Pennsylvania. David Maraniss reconstructs the day through survivor accounts and reporting that paint a vivid picture of the chaos and destruction, as well as how it was seen through the eyes of people living through it in real time.
Read more at The Washington Post
Jennifer Senior’s devastating account of one family’s loss after the attacks won the 2022 Pulitzer Prize for Feature Writing. Bobby McIlvaine was just 26 years old on Sept. 11, 2001, and the story of the different ways his family coped with losing their charming and ambitious son, brother and boyfriend reminds us that grief is unpredictable and personal.
Read more at The Atlantic
Rick Resorla, a former British paratrooper and U.S. Army veteran, was the head of security for Morgan Stanley in the south tower of the World Trade Center. Credited with saving thousands of people, he died when he went back inside to offer more help. This piece by James B. Stewart tells the story of that day through the lens of Resorla’s personal life before the attacks, as well as through his loved ones, who subsequently had to process his heroism and death.
Read more at The New Yorker
This story, published just weeks after 9/11, looks at the lives of five people who were affected by the attacks and how they dealt with the immediate aftermath. A priest delivers a mass, a widow gives her daughter a bath, a firefighter can’t stop thinking of falling bodies. It’s an intimate look at “five people out of the multitudes,” and it stays with you.
Read more at The Washington Post
Windows on the World was a celebrated restaurant at the top of the north tower, and when the first plane hit the building, all escape routes for the 170 employees and patrons who were there that morning were severed. This story, which won a James Beard Award for Best Personal Essay, is told by Cal Sussman, a writer who took a wine class and then became a sommelier at Windows on the World. It works through survivor’s grief and paints a touching portrait of a beloved New York City institution.
Read more at Esquire
Stanley Praimnath and Brian Clark worked on the south tower’s 81st and 84th floors, respectively, and they are two of only four known survivors of the floors above the impact zone. Clark made the fateful decision to go down the only open stairwell, ignoring pleas from others to go up to the roof, and heard Praimnath calling for help. Both reached the ground floor and ran from the building just as it collapsed, and they are still friends to this day.
Read more at The Guardian
This comprehensive retrospective of the first minutes of the attack combines narrative text, photography, video and data journalism to tell the story of what was happening on the ground as the day unfolded. The 17 minutes refers to the time between the first plane hitting the north tower and the second hitting the south one, and reporter Garrett M. Graff highlights a range of accounts from regular people as well as military and government officials about the confusion of that day.
Read more at National Geographic
The post It’s Been 25 Years Since 9/11—These Are the 10 Most Powerful Stories About the Tragedy appeared first on Reader's Digest.

articles.title: You’ll Never Guess How the Football Huddle Got Its Start—Here’s the Fascinating History Behind This Strategy
articles.content:
I firmly believe that the only good thing about the end of summer is the beginning of football season. Though I’m a die-hard New York Giants fan (it’s been a rough few years, but things are gonna turn around!), I’ll watch any and every game I can. On Sundays—and Monday and Thursday nights—from Week 1 through the postseason, you’ll find me near a TV, very likely yelling at the announcers.
But even if the extent of your football knowledge is the name of the team your family roots for, you’ve seen the huddle: The action ends, the players wander back toward one another, and suddenly they’re standing shoulder to shoulder in a little circle. There’s some serious discussion, a few nods, and then they break apart and race to their positions.
It happens over and over, in every football game. It’s such a familiar part of the sport that most of us never stop to wonder about it. But why do football players huddle?
As it turns out, this football staple has a very distinct origin—and it’s one you’d likely never guess. For the deets on one of football’s most recognizable rituals, I turned to two experts: football historian Ken Crippen, founder of the Football Learning Academy, and Jon Kendle, vice president of Archives and Exhibits at the Pro Football Hall of Fame.
Whether you know a blitz from a nickel package or just enjoy the game (or the snacks), we guarantee that you’ll find this fascinating. Read on for the answer before kickoff.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more fun facts, entertainment, humor, travel and tech.
The roots of American football trace back to both soccer and rugby, with the first college football game between Rutgers and Princeton in 1869. In the 1880s, Yale player and coach Walter Camp, who became known as the “father of American football,” helped establish rules that increasingly separated American football from rugby.
The game was barely recognizable by today’s standards. “When it first emerged, forward passing was illegal,” says Crippen. “You would see mass-momentum plays and a lot of physicality.”
And that physicality could be deadly. “So many players died on the field that they would have running counts in the newspapers,” he adds. Football was a game still figuring itself out, from how it was played to how teams communicated in the middle of it.
In the early days of football, quarterbacks simply called or signaled the play—often right at the line of scrimmage. Of course, this “was a problem because the defense could hear the play call,” Crippen notes.
Another option was to call the play while the team was approaching the line of scrimmage, “but far enough away that the defense could not hear them,” he says.
That created an obvious strategic problem: If the defense could hear the play call, it could adjust accordingly. Teams needed a way to communicate without giving away their plans.
The football huddle is widely credited to Gallaudet College, now Gallaudet University, a school for deaf students in Washington, D.C. Gallaudet’s football team was made up of deaf players who communicated using sign language, creating a unique challenge on the field.
Because their opponents were often schools for the hearing-impaired, Gallaudet quarterback Paul Hubbard worried they were watching his hands to read his team’s intentions, according to Kendle. Hubbard’s solution was to form a circle so opponents couldn’t read his signs.
That circle became the first football huddle. The exact game in which it debuted is unknown, but Crippen says the practice appears to have developed organically during Gallaudet’s 1894 season, when the team primarily played the Pennsylvania School for the Deaf and the New York School for the Deaf.
The huddle—which Kendle calls “a magical and special place of trust”—didn’t immediately become a universal part of football.
Amos Alonzo Stagg, one of the sport’s great early innovators, began using the huddle while coaching at the University of Chicago in 1896. But it took a while for the rest of football to catch on. “Stagg was an innovator, and whatever he did was usually copied by other college teams,” Crippen says. Still, the huddle “did not really catch on until the 1920s.”
But the huddle’s usefulness created a new problem: Teams could use it to waste time. “Some saw it as an intentional stall tactic,” Crippen says. That led to rules in the 1930s designed to keep teams from spending too much time in the huddle. Eventually, the introduction of the play clock in 1976 made those restrictions unnecessary. Today, the NFL gives offenses a set amount of time to begin the next play.
Here’s the funny thing: There’s no rule saying a football team needs to huddle. According to the current NFL Rulebook, “a huddle is the action of two or more players in the field of play or in the end zone who, instead of assuming their normal position for the snap, free kick or fair catch kick, form a group for receiving instructions for the next play or for any other reason.”
What happens inside that circle is up to the offense. In a typical huddle, the quarterback communicates instructions for the next play. That, notes Kendle, can “be for the formation, motions, snap count, blocking schemes, wide receiver routes and which gap the running back should run through.”
The huddle also gives the offense a moment to take stock. “It allows the team to see who is hurt, tired or seeing something that the offense can take advantage of against the defense,” Crippen says.
Kendle adds that the huddle can conceal the offense’s formation, making it more difficult for the defense to line up correctly before the snap.
Because sometimes the best way to beat a defense is to deny it time to respond. Enter the no-huddle offense: Rather than gathering to discuss the next play, the offense lines up immediately. The NFL describes it as a strategy that can conserve time, catch the defense off guard and prevent defensive substitutions.
In the 1980s and early 1990s, the Cincinnati Bengals and Buffalo Bills featured “no-huddle” offenses, according to Kendle. The Bills and their “hurry-up” offense advanced to four consecutive Super Bowls.
By the way: No-huddle football is hardly new. Crippen traces its use back to John Heisman (yes, the trophy is named for him), who used the offense at Auburn in 1899.
If the huddle was invented to make communication easier and more secretive, modern technology has made communicating plays much easier.
In the 1940s, Cleveland Browns coach Paul Brown used a “messenger guard” system, in which a substitute player could enter the game with the play from the sideline. Brown also experimented with radio headsets in the 1950s, though it wasn’t until 1994 that the NFL instituted radio helmets to allow limited communication from the sidelines to the quarterback on the field, according to Kendle.
Technology has continued to advance football communication. In 2023, Gallaudet University and AT&T debuted a 5G-connected football helmet that allowed a coach to select a play on a tablet and send it to a digital display inside the quarterback’s helmet.
Probably not—or, at least, not entirely.
“I believe the huddle is still an essential part of football,” Kendle says. “It allows the team to come together as a unit to receive critical instructions and make sure they are on the same page.”
So the next time you watch a football game and see the offense gather around their quarterback, take a second to appreciate what you’re actually looking at. The huddle may look like a simple pause between plays, but it’s one of football’s most enduring strategic tools—giving players a moment to communicate, regroup and figure out what comes next.
Now, if you’ll excuse me, I have a football game to watch.
The post You’ll Never Guess How the Football Huddle Got Its Start—Here’s the Fascinating History Behind This Strategy appeared first on Reader's Digest.

articles.title: Is It Really Rude to Skip the Small Talk and Get Right to the Point?
articles.content:
I consider myself a small-talk connoisseur. We moved a lot when I was a kid, so I had to get good at connecting with strangers quickly or else no one would have shown up to my birthday parties. Now, as an adult, I’m always down to discuss road construction, light news and even the weather (honestly, there’s so much to say about it these days!). Of course, there are times when small talk gets stuck in the “How are you? I’m fine. How are you?” death spiral, but I’d argue that’s just small talk done badly. Not everyone agrees with me—in fact, some people are even calling for the end of small talk, saying that it can be impersonal, a waste of time and even rude.
So I decided to spend a whole day skipping small talk and just opening with whatever deep conversation topic was on my mind. Here’s how it went:
Read on to discover how my little experiment went and find out if it’s really rude to skip small talk these days.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more etiquette, relationships, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
My experiment went … surprisingly OK. I thought people would be taken aback by the abruptness—and maybe they were—but they all engaged. The testosterone count was good, the taro chips were delicious (the cashier and I decided to open the bag and try them together, and they have an aftertaste like Froot Loops), my husband still loves me, and the friendly acquaintance is now closer to a friend because we had a great discussion. My daughter did not agree and said slick-backs are a “classic,” calling out portraits from the 1800s, which is actually a good point.
So maybe the anti–small talk crowd is onto something. This approach is more efficient and clear, and there are so many meaty things to discuss in the world, so why not just get to it?
This preference for just getting to the point may be a cultural shift that’s happening right now. A large majority of Gen Zers in the workforce reported feeling comfortable talking about traditionally taboo topics like job satisfaction and pay with colleagues, according to a recent Adobe Future Workforce Study. And my personal experience with the younger crowd is that this isn’t limited to just workplace conversations—an openness I find refreshing. And hey, I’d rather talk about a stranger’s therapy session than deal with a silent Gen Z stare.
It may also mesh better with more people’s natural inclinations and personalities. Many neurodivergent people report small talk as feeling performative and draining, making social interactions even more difficult. And once they said it, many neurotypical people found they agreed. As a friend with autism put it: “It’s hard enough to figure out what to say to you. Now I have to figure out fake stuff to say first?” Plus, small talk can sometimes come across as fake, making you doubt the motives of the person speaking it.
Lastly, science says ditching the small talk actually works. In another study, researchers put people into two groups: one that had strangers engage in shallow small talk, and another where strangers had deep conversations. They asked the participants to rate how awkward the situation felt, and as it turns out, all the conversations ended up less awkward than expected. But the surprising part is that the biggest gap in expectation was in the group with deep conversations—meaning the conversations people were most afraid would go wrong actually went the most right. The risk paid off.
The one instance where my experiment went painfully awry was when I skipped the small talk with my new co-worker and told her about my sketchy breakfast. She immediately redirected me back to small talk with “So I’m Jane—it’s nice to meet you.” And while my husband did answer me, he looked worried and asked if we could have a longer conversation. A little small-talk prelude might have prevented his worry.
Small talk exists for a reason: to bridge the gap between not conversing and conversing. There are so many factors that determine how people communicate, and small talk is a way to feel each other out first. This gives the conversation a better chance at being successful. To skip the small talk, you either have to ignore many of those factors or make some wild assumptions and hope you’re right. People who say they don’t like small talk because it feels fake (“No one really cares how I’m doing; why do they even bother asking me?”) may not realize that the purpose of the small talk isn’t the answer, per se, but the interaction.
And for people with neurodivergence or those who just struggle when conversing, small talk can be helpful by providing a predictable script and an on-ramp to a conversation, reducing overall anxiety. I think it’s more anxiety-producing to have someone ask you a deep question out of the blue. Small talk can prevent a conversation from oversharing or veering into trauma dumping. Who hasn’t had an acquaintance tell them something catastrophic and not known how to answer?
My last case for small talk: Saying something, anything, is better than saying nothing. Small talk is designed to be a simple, bite-sized, recognizable way to connect. And we need that. We live in a world where we drive straight into our garages and close the door without ever saying hi to a neighbor. Where we are on social media for hours but are never social. Where we “talk” to people online but hardly ever do so in real life. People are lonely, and we need real, in-person connections—even if that is “just small talk.”

The right amount of small talk is somewhere between zero and the whole conversation. The trick is to pay attention to the cues the other person is giving you. If they seem like they’re in a hurry or withdrawing, keep small talk to a minimum. If it seems like they need more time to warm up and feel comfortable talking, add in a little more. Small talk is a learned skill, and the more you do it, the better you’ll get at spotting these cues.

I consider myself a small-talk connoisseur. We moved a lot when I was a kid, so I had to get good at connecting with strangers quickly or else no one would have shown up to my birthday parties. Now, as an adult, I’m always down to discuss road construction, light news and even the weather (honestly, there’s so much to say about it these days!). Of course, there are times when small talk gets stuck in the “How are you? I’m fine. How are you?” death spiral, but I’d argue that’s just small talk done badly. Not everyone agrees with me—in fact, some people are even calling for the end of small talk, saying that it can be impersonal, a waste of time and even rude.

So I decided to spend a whole day skipping small talk and just opening with whatever deep conversation topic was on my mind. Here’s how it went:

  • To a friend at the gym: “Hey, how are the testosterone injections going? What’s your sperm count at now?”
  • To a cashier at Costco: “Do you think Lay’s is going too far with selling this 2-pound bag of chili-lime taro chips? That seems like a bold move to go straight to the bulk size when most people couldn’t identify taro on a produce chart.”
  • To my husband: “The fact that the dishes are in the sink and not the dishwasher makes me wonder if you truly love me, and now I’m questioning our relationship.”
  • To my daughter: “Severely parted, slicked-back ponytails are going to be the big thing your generation cringes at when they look back on their teen years. After ‘6-7,’ of course.”
  • To a friendly acquaintance: “I watched a YouTube essay about why Gen Zers aren’t having kids, and I keep thinking about it. Do you think your kids are planning on having children?” (Her kids are 4 and 8.)
  • To a newish work colleague: “I ate a breakfast sandwich one week past its expiration date this morning. Not sure that was the wisest choice.”

Read on to discover how my little experiment went and find out if it’s really rude to skip small talk these days.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more etiquette, relationships, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.

The case for skipping small talk

My experiment went … surprisingly OK. I thought people would be taken aback by the abruptness—and maybe they were—but they all engaged. The testosterone count was good, the taro chips were delicious (the cashier and I decided to open the bag and try them together, and they have an aftertaste like Froot Loops), my husband still loves me, and the friendly acquaintance is now closer to a friend because we had a great discussion. My daughter did not agree and said slick-backs are a “classic,” calling out portraits from the 1800s, which is actually a good point.

So maybe the anti–small talk crowd is onto something. This approach is more efficient and clear, and there are so many meaty things to discuss in the world, so why not just get to it?

This preference for just getting to the point may be a cultural shift that’s happening right now. A large majority of Gen Zers in the workforce reported feeling comfortable talking about traditionally taboo topics like job satisfaction and pay with colleagues, according to a recent Adobe Future Workforce Study. And my personal experience with the younger crowd is that this isn’t limited to just workplace conversations—an openness I find refreshing. And hey, I’d rather talk about a stranger’s therapy session than deal with a silent Gen Z stare.

It may also mesh better with more people’s natural inclinations and personalities. Many neurodivergent people report small talk as feeling performative and draining, making social interactions even more difficult. And once they said it, many neurotypical people found they agreed. As a friend with autism put it: “It’s hard enough to figure out what to say to you. Now I have to figure out fake stuff to say first?” Plus, small talk can sometimes come across as fake, making you doubt the motives of the person speaking it.

Lastly, science says ditching the small talk actually works. In another study, researchers put people into two groups: one that had strangers engage in shallow small talk, and another where strangers had deep conversations. They asked the participants to rate how awkward the situation felt, and as it turns out, all the conversations ended up less awkward than expected. But the surprising part is that the biggest gap in expectation was in the group with deep conversations—meaning the conversations people were most afraid would go wrong actually went the most right. The risk paid off.

The case for keeping small talk

The one instance where my experiment went painfully awry was when I skipped the small talk with my new co-worker and told her about my sketchy breakfast. She immediately redirected me back to small talk with “So I’m Jane—it’s nice to meet you.” And while my husband did answer me, he looked worried and asked if we could have a longer conversation. A little small-talk prelude might have prevented his worry.

Small talk exists for a reason: to bridge the gap between not conversing and conversing. There are so many factors that determine how people communicate, and small talk is a way to feel each other out first. This gives the conversation a better chance at being successful. To skip the small talk, you either have to ignore many of those factors or make some wild assumptions and hope you’re right. People who say they don’t like small talk because it feels fake (“No one really cares how I’m doing; why do they even bother asking me?”) may not realize that the purpose of the small talk isn’t the answer, per se, but the interaction.

And for people with neurodivergence or those who just struggle when conversing, small talk can be helpful by providing a predictable script and an on-ramp to a conversation, reducing overall anxiety. I think it’s more anxiety-producing to have someone ask you a deep question out of the blue. Small talk can prevent a conversation from oversharing or veering into trauma dumping. Who hasn’t had an acquaintance tell them something catastrophic and not known how to answer?

My last case for small talk: Saying something, anything, is better than saying nothing. Small talk is designed to be a simple, bite-sized, recognizable way to connect. And we need that. We live in a world where we drive straight into our garages and close the door without ever saying hi to a neighbor. Where we are on social media for hours but are never social. Where we “talk” to people online but hardly ever do so in real life. People are lonely, and we need real, in-person connections—even if that is “just small talk.”

It depends who you’re talking to

The need for small talk depends on a variety of factors:

  • Relationship: If the person is a complete stranger, like a grocery bagger, then small talk really is the best option because you don’t know anything about them and likely won’t have further interaction. However, if you’re speaking to your mom or your best friend, you can just answer the phone with “I found a lump.”
  • Location: Small talk works best in light social situations in public, like a store, gym, church or school. Workplaces often prefer efficiency and may prefer less small talk. However, there is also a place for small talk in more intimate settings, like a first date or family reunion.
  • Purpose: Ask yourself what the goal for the conversation is. Are you trying to have a brief positive interaction with a stranger? Feel out a connection with a potential friend or partner? Talk to an old friend? Small talk can be the entire interaction or the bridge that leads to something deeper.
  • Topic: If you’re delivering emergency information, skip the small talk and spit it out. If you’re sharing bad or sad information, consider a few buffering sentences. If you’re sharing something awesome, you can probably just blurt it out. If you’re asking someone else a question, it’s probably best to warm them up first.
  • Age: Older people were taught that small talk was polite and expected, so not using any may come across as rude or jarring, even if you don’t mean it that way. Similarly, many younger people find it off-putting, so if you’re looking to connect, try following their conversational lead.

The bottom line: Whether skipping the small talk comes across as rude or transactional depends mostly on your tone and your relationship with the other person.

How much small talk is actually enough

The right amount of small talk is somewhere between zero and the whole conversation. The trick is to pay attention to the cues the other person is giving you. If they seem like they’re in a hurry or withdrawing, keep small talk to a minimum. If it seems like they need more time to warm up and feel comfortable talking, add in a little more. Small talk is a learned skill, and the more you do it, the better you’ll get at spotting these cues.

Again, this number depends heavily on the above factors. For instance, an informal LinkedIn poll found that 78% of professionals want small talk limited to under two minutes in meetings.

In my opinion, a good rule of thumb across the spectrum of conversation types would be somewhere between 20 seconds and five minutes.

How to skip small talk without being a jerk about it

My experiment showed me that there really isn’t a smooth way to skip the small talk entirely. People will generally roll with you, but coming right out of the gate with “Bobarino, I need last quarter’s numbers by 2 p.m.” or “Your child can’t read and needs a tutor” is going to feel aggressive to most people unless you temper it a little. So here’s how to skip small talk the right way:

  • Use a tiny bit of small talk. I know, I know. But just a quick “Hey, it’s good to see you—how’s it going?” is often enough.
  • Keep your tone warm and polite.
  • Use the “pivot technique” by bringing up a more casual but related topic, and then after a minute or two, pivot to the thing you really wanted to discuss.
  • Check in with the other person regularly by watching for signs that they’re uncomfortable or by asking them directly.
  • Allow the other person to talk. Skipping small talk isn’t an excuse to monologue at someone.

The verdict

Skipping small talk isn’t inherently rude. Small talk exists as an entry point to a conversation, and if you have a funnier, more interesting or more relevant conversation starter, then by all means use that. The difference between “great conversationalist” and “rude jerk” will be in your tone and care for the other person during the conversation.

That said, it’s also never rude to use a little bit of small talk to help everyone feel comfortable. So next time I see my gym friend, I’m going to go with “Hey, how’s your health these days? The testosterone injections still helping?”
